chief_complaint: severe body aches, goosebumps, diarrhea, tearing, and pupil dilation 16 hours after last heroin use
hpi_details: He injects heroin and fentanyl and last used an opioid about 16 hours ago. He now has body aches, piloerection, lacrimation, mydriasis, and diarrhea; COWS score is 16, consistent with moderate opioid withdrawal. He requests treatment for opioid use disorder and relief of withdrawal symptoms.
ideas: He believes he is in opioid withdrawal and wants help stopping safely.
concerns: He fears severe withdrawal and overdose if he returns to use.
expectations: He wants medication for opioid use disorder, naloxone, and follow-up support.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Opioid Use Disorder OUD Withdrawal and Buprenorphine Induction evaluation and management
core_concepts: Opioid withdrawal is diagnosed clinically from a compatible history and objective signs; COWS supports assessment of severity but should not replace examination and clinical judgment.

Buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal if given before sufficient spontaneous withdrawal. Recent fentanyl exposure can make timing less predictable, so use observed clinical withdrawal and an individualized induction plan.
Medication for opioid use disorder reduces overdose risk. Offer buprenorphine or referral for methadone as appropriate, overdose education, take-home naloxone, and linkage to ongoing treatment.

Assess co-use of alcohol, benzodiazepines, sedatives, stimulants, and other opioids, as well as depression, suicide risk, withdrawal complications, intoxication, and capacity to engage in outpatient care.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe body aches, goosebumps, diarrhea, tearing, and pupil dilation 16 hours after last heroin use
Key HPI features: injection heroin and fentanyl use, last opioid use about 16 hours ago, COWS 16, body aches, piloerection, lacrimation, mydriasis, and diarrhea.

Objective/Exam findings: obtain vital signs, repeat withdrawal assessment, assess mental status and hydration, inspect injection sites when appropriate, and evaluate for intoxication, infection, and withdrawal from alcohol or sedatives.
common_misconceptions: Detoxification alone treats opioid use disorder or protects against later overdose.
A fixed number of hours since last use is sufficient to start buprenorphine regardless of symptoms or fentanyl exposure.
Opioid withdrawal is usually fatal; its major immediate danger is return to use with reduced tolerance and overdose risk.
Naloxone is unnecessary once medication for opioid use disorder is started.
dangerous_errors: Giving standard buprenorphine induction before adequate objective withdrawal, especially after fentanyl exposure, and failing to recognize or treat precipitated withdrawal.
Missing respiratory depression or sedation from opioid or sedative co-use, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, delirium, sepsis, or severe dehydration.
Failing to assess suicide, self-harm, violence risk, capacity, or inability to care for self before outpatient disposition.
Discharging without overdose counseling, naloxone, safer-use advice, and timely linkage to continuing medication treatment.
management_principles: Confirm moderate, observable opioid withdrawal and clinical stability before a standard buprenorphine induction; use an individualized or specialist-supported pathway when fentanyl exposure, uncertainty, or prior precipitated withdrawal complicates induction.
Monitor symptoms, vital signs, sedation, hydration, and response during induction; treat gastrointestinal and autonomic symptoms supportively as appropriate.
Provide naloxone and education that tolerance falls after abstinence; advise avoiding use alone and combining opioids with alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other sedatives.
Link directly to ongoing medication treatment, counseling and harm-reduction services, and evaluate injection-related HIV, hepatitis, and skin or bloodstream infection risks.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Escalate to emergency care for respiratory depression, severe intoxication, delirium, uncontrolled vomiting or dehydration, suspected sepsis, severe alcohol or sedative withdrawal, or an unsafe psychiatric presentation.

Medication selection and induction method require local protocol and clinician assessment; pregnancy, liver disease, pain treatment, co-prescribed sedatives, and inability to follow up may alter the plan.

reference_soap.subjective: 31-year-old man who injects heroin and fentanyl, last using an opioid about 16 hours ago, with body aches, piloerection, lacrimation, mydriasis, and diarrhea. COWS is 16. Assess co-use of sedatives and alcohol, overdose history, injection complications, suicide and self-harm risk, and readiness for ongoing treatment.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain vital signs, mental-status examination, serial withdrawal assessments, hydration status, and focused examination for intoxication, sedation, infection, and injection-site complications. Use targeted tests for suspected medical complications.
reference_soap.assessment: Moderate opioid withdrawal in the setting of opioid use disorder. Consider sedative or alcohol withdrawal, intoxication, infection, gastroenteritis, and other medical causes of autonomic or gastrointestinal symptoms.
reference_soap.plan: If clinically stable and in adequate observable withdrawal, begin an individualized buprenorphine induction according to local protocol, with extra caution after fentanyl exposure and monitoring for precipitated withdrawal. Provide naloxone, overdose and safer-use counseling, infection screening or prevention as indicated, and direct linkage to ongoing medication treatment. Escalate for respiratory depression, delirium, severe co-withdrawal, sepsis, dehydration, or acute safety risk.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Opioid Use Disorder OUD Withdrawal and Buprenorphine Induction
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for severe body aches, goosebumps, diarrhea, tearing, and pupil dilation 16 hours after last heroin use
Plan safe buprenorphine induction and overdose prevention while recognizing conditions requiring emergency escalation
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.diagnosis: Opioid Use Disorder OUD Withdrawal and Buprenorphine Induction
teaching.one_liner: Moderate opioid withdrawal in a man injecting heroin and fentanyl, requiring assessment for safe medication initiation, co-occurring withdrawal or illness, and overdose prevention.
red_flags: Respiratory depression, marked sedation, or suspected overdose
Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, delirium, sepsis, severe dehydration, or inability to maintain safety

must_ask.say: How much heroin or fentanyl have you been using, and when was your last use?
Are you having body aches, chills, goosebumps, or diarrhea right now?
Do you inject the drug, and how often do you use it each day?
Have you tried methadone or buprenorphine treatment before, and did it help?
Have you ever overdosed, or used alone where no one could help you?
Have you recently used alcohol, benzodiazepines such as Xanax or Valium, or other sedating medicines?
Have you had thoughts of suicide, self-harm, or harming anyone else, or do you feel too unwell to keep yourself safe today?

history.answer: I am trying to stop using heroin, but I have terrible body aches all over and I feel sick.
I inject heroin mixed with fentanyl into my arms about three to four times a day, usually around half a gram to a gram total each day.
I started taking prescription pain pills about four years ago, and switched to shooting heroin two years ago because my tolerance went way up.
I last used about sixteen hours ago, late last night.
I have tried cutting back many times, but the cravings get so intense that I always end up using more than I intended.
history.topic: Attempts to cut down and cravings

history.answer: I do not really drink alcohol, maybe one beer every few months socially, so drinking has never been a problem for me.
I lost my previous job because I was calling in sick when withdrawing, and I have spent most of my savings to keep using, though I have never been arrested or driven while high.
history.topic: Impact on daily life and safety

history.answer: My muscles and bones ache terribly, I have goosebumps and chills, my eyes keep watering, and I have had severe diarrhea twice this morning.
No, I have never had seizures, hallucinations, or delirium during withdrawal.
I had an accidental overdose about a year ago and woke up in the ER after someone gave me naloxone.
I always use clean needles from a local syringe exchange and never share equipment, and my last hepatitis and HIV tests six months ago were negative.
No, I have never had yellow skin, threw up blood, had black stools, or had severe stomach pains.
I do not take sleeping pills, Xanax, or other benzodiazepines, and I do not use stimulants like cocaine or meth.
I feel anxious and down about where my life is right now, but I have never thought about ending my life or hurting myself.
I went to an outpatient detox program about eight months ago, but I relapsed within two weeks because I did not stay on any maintenance medication.
I want to stop because I am terrified of dying from an overdose, and I really want to regain control of my health and life.
I live alone in an apartment, but my sister lives nearby and is very supportive of me getting help today.
I know I am going through withdrawal right now, and I want medical help to get through it safely without relapsing.
I am afraid the withdrawal will get unbearable, and I fear that if I leave here without treatment, I will use again and overdose.
I am hoping to start medication like buprenorphine today, get a prescription for naloxone, and connect with ongoing treatment.
I was diagnosed with high blood pressure and slightly high cholesterol two years ago.
I had an appendectomy when I was seventeen, with no complications.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure, and nothing else.
I have no known drug allergies.
I do not smoke cigarettes or vape.
I currently work part-time in warehouse logistics and live by myself in a rented apartment.
My father has hypertension and my mother has type 2 diabetes, but there is no family history of substance use disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and temperature 37.1°C.
Appears restless and visibly uncomfortable, shifting frequently in the chair with noticeable goosebumps and sweating.
Sclerae are anicteric and conjunctivae are clear without pallor or jaundice.
Pupils are symmetrically dilated at 6 mm, reactive to light, with prominent lacrimation bilaterally, and extraocular movements are intact.
Clear rhinorrhea present; oral mucosa is mildly dry without lesions or pharyngeal erythema.
Tachycardic with regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2, and no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Hyperactive bowel sounds heard across all four quadrants.
Abdomen is soft and non-distended without tenderness, guarding, or rigidity.
No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, and no signs of ascites.
Piloerection and diaphoresis present; several healed and clean venous puncture marks on both forearms without erythema, warmth, or abscess.
Mild bilateral postural hand tremor and motor restlessness without involuntary jerks.
Alert and fully oriented to person, place, and time, with intact attention and linear thought process despite marked physical discomfort.
Gait is steady and coordination is preserved without ataxia or stumbling.
